summary.title: Missed best friend's wedding as best man
summary.what_happened: I was supposed to be my best friend's best man. Three days before the wedding, my boss asked me to cover a client trip and I said yes. I told him by text, so he had to find another best man at the last minute. Afterwards I sent a gift and said sorry once by text. He has been cold to me since the wedding. It has been four months.
summary.my_needs: The client was a big one and my promotion is coming up, and I feel he knows how important my career is to me.
summary.desired_outcome: I want things to go back to normal.

consult.text:
Four months of distance from a close friend is hard, especially when you want things to go back to normal. It makes sense that this hurts, and that your work pressure was real.

Here is how he may see it. He asked you to stand next to him on one of the biggest days of his life. Three days before, he learned by text that you would not be there, and he had to find another best man quickly. Even if he understands your job, the way and the timing may have felt like he came second. One apology by text may not feel like enough.

The main issue here seems to be that you chose work over his wedding and told him in a way that left him almost no time. That is not about your ambition being wrong. It is about the impact on him.

What we don't know is what he has actually said about it, or what would feel like repair to him.

Some next steps:
1. Offer a call or a meeting, not a text, to listen to how the wedding was for him.
2. Say plainly that missing it was your choice and that it hurt him, without explaining why first.
3. Ask what he needs from you now.
I already apologised. What more does he want, me to quit my job?

It sounds frustrating to feel you have already said sorry and to still be met with distance. I don't think he needs you to quit your job.

What I said before still stands, in gentler words. Missing the wedding and telling him by text was a big thing to take on, and a short written apology may not have matched it. That is not about whether you are allowed to have a career. It is about how it landed for him.

What he wants is unknown. That is the useful question. Nobody can tell from outside whether he wants a longer conversation, to be heard, or simply time.

You could:
1. Ask him for a call or a coffee to hear how that day was for him.
2. Listen first, before you explain your work reasons.
3. Tell him you would like to repair things, and ask what would help.

share_draft: Hi. I want to talk about your wedding. I was meant to be your best man, and I let you down. Three days before, I chose to cover a client trip and I told you by text. That left you very little time to find someone else, and I'm sorry for that. My short apology by text did not feel like enough, and I'd like to do better. I miss our friendship and I would like things to feel normal between us again. Would you be open to talking, in whichever way suits you, about how this has been for you?
